response:
To explain the concept of parallel lines in hyperbolic geometry, we need to delve into the unique properties of this non-Euclidean geometry.

### Understanding Hyperbolic Geometry

In hyperbolic geometry, the parallel postulate of Euclidean geometry (which states that through any point not on a given line, exactly one line can be drawn parallel to the given line) is replaced by the following axiom:

**Axiom of Hyperbolic Parallelism**: For any line L and any point P not on L, there exist two lines through P that are parallel to L.

### Poincaré Disk Model

The Poincaré disk model is a common way to represent hyperbolic geometry. In this model:
- Points are represented as points inside a unit disk.
- Lines are represented as circles that are perpendicular to the boundary of the disk.

### Definition of Parallel Lines in Hyperbolic Geometry

In the Poincaré disk model:
- Two lines are parallel if they are tangent to the same circle of the disk.

### Intuitive Example

Consider the unit disk in the Poincaré disk model. Take any line (which appears as a circle perpendicular to the boundary of the disk) and a point P not on this line. By the axiom of hyperbolic parallelism, there exist at least two lines through P that are parallel to the given line. These lines will appear as circles through P and tangent to the original line.

### Conclusion

The concept of parallel lines in hyperbolic geometry is fundamentally different from that in Euclidean geometry. In hyperbolic geometry, there are multiple lines (or circles) that can pass through a point and be parallel to a given line, reflecting the non-existence of a unique parallel line in this context.

\[
\text{The Poincaré disk model, with lines represented as circles perpendicular to the boundary, illustrates the existence of multiple parallel lines through a point.}
\]
